2422.tx: A regular filter coffee costs a fraction of what a Starbucks cup does, yet the queues outside its stores rarely thin out. That gap between price and demand is really the starting point for understanding the Starbucks business model. Starbucks is not just selling coffee; it is selling convenience, customisation and a recognisable brand experience wrapped around every cup. Company-operated stores, licensed outlets, packaged products, a loyalty programme and a mobile app all pull in the same direction, and each piece adds its own layer to the wider Starbucks revenue model that keeps the company growing even in a tough year for consumer spending. This piece breaks down how Starbucks makes money, why its business strategy leans so heavily on scale and repeat purchases, and where the model is now being tested by rising costs and slower footfall. Ellis argues that the investment landscape has changed significantly over the decades, making it increasingly difficult for individual investors to consistently outperform the broader market. His philosophy challenges the belief that investors must constantly search for winning stocks or trade actively to build wealth. Instead, he emphasises the importance of recognising personal limitations, managing risks and sticking to a well-defined investment strategy.
